title: HoloPart: Generative 3D Part Amodal Segmentation
one_liner: HoloPart uses a diffusion model with two kinds of selective focus to infer hidden parts of 3D objects by reasoning about the whole shape.
lead: When you see a 3D object from one angle, many parts are hidden from view. HoloPart teaches a model to imagine and complete those hidden parts by reasoning about the complete shape. It does this in two stages: first, segment visible surfaces; second, use a diffusion model (a step-by-step generator that refines random noise into shapes) with two kinds of selective focus (looking closely at local details AND looking at how the part fits in the whole) to fill in the hidden surfaces while keeping the whole object consistent.

paras: Today's 3D segmentation models (which carve 3D shapes into named parts like handle, bowl, base) only identify what is visible. They see a cup from one side and label the outer walls, but ignore the interior, the bottom, and the hidden rim. This is fine if you only care about the visible surface, but useless for 3D content creation: animators need full parts, modelers need complete surfaces, and material assignment needs hidden areas.

A beginner might try to guess hidden surfaces with simple rules (flip the visible surface, or assume a standard shape). This breaks because objects have wildly different interiors. A car door hides complex hinges; a strawberry hides seeds; a bowl hides an inner curve that does not mirror its outside.

callout.html: A generative model learns to fill in hidden surfaces of incomplete 3D parts by imagining what lies underneath while respecting how the whole object must fit together.

panels.title: 1. Partial Scan
panels.caption: Scanner sees one side of a 3D object. Hidden parts remain unknown.

panels.title: 2. Surface Segmentation

panels.caption: Existing algorithm segments visible surfaces into semantic parts.

panels.title: 3. Local Detail Focus
panels.caption: Zoom in on each part's edges, boundaries, and fine details.

panels.title: 5. Complete Part

steps.text: Learn a foundation model by training on intact 3D objects, learning to compress them into compressed codes (short lists of numbers).
Take the incomplete visible surface and convert it into a compressed code using two channels that see both the part and the full shape.
Zoom in: look at the part's edges, boundaries, and local curves in isolation.
Zoom out: check that the part fits the whole object's size, orientation, and connections.
Repeat and refine the compressed code by gradually removing noise, converging to a complete, consistent part.

paras: HoloPart changes the compressed codes (short lists of numbers that represent 3D shapes). These codes are the internal numbers a neural network uses to describe and recreate 3D objects. Instead of accepting incomplete codes derived from visible surfaces only, HoloPart refines and extends them to represent the full, hidden part.

hidden.h2: The Hidden Quantity: Part Completion Coherence
hidden.name: Part completion coherence score
paras: The paper implicitly measures how well the inferred hidden surfaces respect both local detail and global object structure. This is not a single number the authors explicitly name, but rather a balance: locally, does the generated surface follow the part's natural edges and bends? Globally, does it connect properly to neighboring parts and fit the whole object's shape? The model achieves this through two pathways: one pathway examines fine local details, while the other pathway grounds each local decision against the whole shape.

The paper measures this coherence indirectly via Chamfer Distance (how far the generated surface is from the true hidden surface), IoU (what fraction of the complete part the model correctly predicts), F-Score (a mix of precision and recall), and Success Rate (did the model produce a valid, non-degenerate surface?). These metrics all assume that a high-quality completion is one where the generated surface sits close to the true hidden part and connects consistently with the rest of the object.

heat.caption: Darker means the model must reason about that aspect to complete the part well. Highlighted cells are what the two focus pathways directly address.

reads.html: Both local details and global context matter equally. A perfect inferred surface looks right up close AND connects to the whole object without gaps or contradictions.
Two selective focus pathways work together: one learns the global shape structure, while the other preserves fine local details and ensures the position is correct.

mechanism.h2: Why Two Kinds of Focus Complete Hidden Parts
paras: The core challenge is that a hidden surface has no ground-truth pixels or sensor data. The model must imagine it. But pure imagination can produce nonsense: an interior curve that contradicts the exterior, or a part size that breaks the whole. HoloPart solves this by reasoning in two channels simultaneously.

Local focus acts like a magnifying glass on the visible patch. It studies the visible edges, their bends, their thickness, their texture, and extrapolates inward. A coffee mug's rim has a specific lip profile; the local pathway learns that profile from visible data and extends it to the hidden interior, because most curved edges continue smoothly underneath.

But local focus alone hallucinates: it might generate an interior that is physically impossible, too thick, or the wrong size. Global focus prevents this by anchoring every local decision to the whole shape. It asks: given the complete object's size, symmetry, and structure, what interior makes sense? This constrains the local guesses to solutions that fit the whole. The result is a hidden surface that is both locally detailed and globally consistent.

stages.s: Compress part and shape into short number lists
Local focus: study visible edges and surfaces
Global focus: check that part fits in whole
Complete part with hidden surfaces inferred

math.words: global_output = focus_on_whole_shape(part_code, full_shape_code) + local_output = focus_on_local_details(part_code) + final_code = global_output + local_output
math.equation:
z_complete = LocalFocus(z_part) + GlobalFocus(z_part, z_shape)

where z_part is the compressed code for the visible part, z_shape is the compressed code for the whole object, and the two focus outputs are summed to produce z_complete, the compressed code for the full completed part.
symbols: compressed number-list representing the visible part
compressed number-list of the whole 3D object
output compressed code for the complete part
pathway that links to the global shape
both pathways contribute equally to the result

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Imagine a coffee mug with the rim and bottom hidden. z_part encodes the visible outer wall (maybe 10 numbers in a list).
z_shape encodes the whole mug learned from training data (maybe 50 numbers in a list).
LocalFocus zooms in: it sees the wall thickness is 0.5 millimeters, the lip profile curves inward at 20 degrees. It produces a 10-number update suggesting how the hidden interior should curve.
GlobalFocus zooms out: it sees the whole mug is 8 centimeters tall, 6 centimeters wide, and should be symmetric. It produces a 10-number update that ensures the interior fits those constraints.
Final z_complete = LocalFocus output (10 numbers) + GlobalFocus output (10 numbers) = 20-number combined code that represents the full rim and bottom, locally detailed and globally consistent.

math.note: Both pathways contribute equally in the sum; this ensures fine details do not override global constraints, and vice versa.

bars.h2: Completion Quality: Two-Focus Method vs Baselines

charts.title: Naive: Mirror visible surface
charts.note: Mirroring assumes symmetry, but most parts have different interiors from exteriors. Many interiors cannot be guessed by flipping. Distance stays high because the guess is systematically wrong.

charts.title: Local focus only (no global check)
charts.note: Fine local details improve, but without checking the global shape, the part often misaligns with its neighbors or produces impossible topologies (e.g., overlapping surfaces). This happens because local focus does not reason about the whole.

charts.title: HoloPart: Both foci working together
charts.note: Local and global pathways together produce surfaces that are both finely detailed and aligned with the whole shape, because each pathway constrains the other.

items.html: If local focus dominates, the model invents plausible-looking but wrong interior details. A table leg might fill with intricate carvings that do not exist, because the local pathways sees a carved outer surface and extrapolates, with no global check.

If global focus is too strong, the model locks the interior to a generic average, erasing true variation. A bowl might homogenize all interiors to a single smooth curve, because the global pathways over-constrains to match a template.

The model trains only on complete objects. If a test object is radically different from all training shapes, both pathways fail: local pathways have no examples of that edge type, and global pathways cannot find a matching template.

Both pathways carry equal weight and train together on complete shapes. The model learns to trust local cues for small variations and global cues for large structure, because both corrections flow together during training.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Download a 3D model library (e.g., ShapeNet or ABO with models of chairs, mugs, bowls), hide a random part of each object from view, run HoloPart to infer the hidden surfaces, and measure how close the inferred surfaces are to the true hidden parts. Compare three approaches: (A) naive mirror, (B) local focus only, (C) HoloPart with both foci. Plot the distance-to-truth on a bar chart and show 3D side-by-side pictures of the inferred parts for at least two test objects.
demo.metric_eq: completion_score = (1 - (distance_to_truth / maximum_possible_distance)) * 100; ranges 0-100, higher is better
demo.closing: The demo must show that two foci together produce surfaces closer to reality and more coherent than either focus alone, especially on objects the model has never seen before training.
